clue.text: Serving of risotto’s for German lad (4)

indicators.note: A serving is a portion dished out of something bigger, so only a stretch of the word that follows is wanted.

blocks.note: four consecutive letters sit inside this one word, starting at its third letter

explanation.surface: A plate of rice being dished up for a boy from Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Serving of' belongs to the restaurant picture and is also the instruction; the letters are already lying in order inside the dish, needing nothing done to them.
explanation.definitionFit: Otto is a standard German boy's name — Bismarck's first name — so the definition points at a forename rather than at anything to do with rice.

clue.text: Combatants of Chester mustered (3,6)

indicators.note: Troops are mustered when they are called together and drawn up in a fresh formation, which is what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: nine letters of raw material, the little joining word included, coming out in another order

explanation.surface: Soldiers from a Cheshire city being called out on parade.
explanation.walkthrough: The city name does no geographical work at all; it is nine letters of fodder, and the 'of' that looks like grammar goes into the shuffle with it.
explanation.definitionFit: The forces are the army, navy and air force taken together — the people whose job is fighting, which is what 'combatants' names.

clue.text: Love Prince? He will get love interest afflicted principally: her (7)

definitions.note: The definition is the bare pronoun 'her', which would fit any woman at all; the prince and the afflicted love interest in the wordplay are what narrow it to one.

indicators.note: Principally means chiefly or at the head, so the leading letter of each word it governs is all that is taken.

blocks.note: a score of love in tennis is nothing, and nothing is written as a nought
P is the standard abbreviation for prince, and the question mark admits it is a squeeze
the clue's own pronoun, used exactly as it stands
the opening letter of each of these three words, in the order printed

explanation.surface: A prince's romance going badly wrong for the woman caught up in it.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare is never named: a prince and a love interest driven out of her wits are all the pointing the clue does, and both of those words are wordplay as well.
explanation.definitionFit: 'her' works only with the clue's prince and madness around it, narrowing the pronoun to Hamlet's love, who loses her reason and drowns.

clue.text: Nitwit in protective cover taken aback (4)

indicators.note: To be taken aback is to be knocked backwards, and in an across entry backwards means read from the right-hand end.

blocks.note: a tarp is the waterproof sheet thrown over whatever has to stay dry, and those four letters are then read from the far end

explanation.surface: An idiot startled while sheltering under a tarpaulin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken aback' is surprise in the surface and a direction of travel in the wordplay, which is the only thing hiding a very ordinary four-letter word.
explanation.definitionFit: A prat is a fool in ordinary British usage — the mild insult you throw at someone who has just done something silly.

clue.text: Elite soldier having hissy fit in defensive structure (7)

blocks.note: a para is a paratrooper, one of the airborne troops
to be in a pet is to be in a sulk — an old British word for a fit of temper, nothing to do with animals

explanation.surface: A crack soldier throwing a tantrum up on the battlements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pet' meaning a sulk has almost left speech and survives in the phrase 'in a pet', and nothing in the clue warns you that the family cat is not wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A parapet is the low wall running along the top of a rampart or roof that soldiers shelter behind, so it is both defensive and a structure.

clue.text: Something unpleasant afoot? No, a treat for Piglet (5)

blocks.note: the setter withdraws the foot reading with 'No' and hands over the little word beside it exactly as printed
the hard painful patch a walker gets on a toe, which is what 'afoot' pins the fragment to

explanation.surface: A foot complaint being ruled out in favour of something a small pig would enjoy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Afoot' sets up the toe complaint and the comma then throws it away, because the same letters read as one word rather than two are a thing to eat.
explanation.definitionFit: Piglet, in Winnie-the-Pooh, is forever after acorns — he calls them haycorns — so the definition names the answer by who eats it.

clue.text: Decide against show of emotion: that’s rotten (3,3)

blocks.note: tears are the most obvious show of emotion there is
milk that has gone off has gone bad, which is the British way of saying food is rotten

explanation.surface: Ruling out a display of tears on the grounds that it is a rotten thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon does the work of an equals sign, so the sentence reads as a moral judgement while it is quietly a sum, and 'rotten' points at food rather than at behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: To cry off is to back out of something you had already agreed to do, which is deciding against it after the fact.

clue.text: Give another grade to statement (6)

blocks.note: an examiner going over a script a second time does exactly this, and the hyphen the sense needs has been left off on purpose
the everyday noun for something said in passing

explanation.surface: A teacher being asked to grade a written statement all over again.
explanation.walkthrough: One printed word covers two unrelated ones, kept apart only by a hyphen that is missing: with it an examiner's job, without it a thing somebody said.
explanation.definitionFit: To re-mark a paper is to grade it again, while a remark is an aside — the same six letters covering an examiner's task and a scrap of speech.

clue.text: Rescuers here for nonsensical update (9,6)

indicators.note: Something nonsensical makes no sense as written, so the words in front of it are not to be read in the order they stand.

blocks.note: fifteen letters of raw material across three words, coming out in a new order

explanation.surface: A caption saying where the rescue party is and what they have come about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rescuers here for' reads like the start of a news bulletin, and every letter of it is fodder — including the 'for' that looks like nothing but joinery.
explanation.definitionFit: A refresher course is training taken to bring worn knowledge back up to date, so 'update' names it by what it does to the person on it.

clue.text: OK? Not quite: demon gin drunk in children’s film (7,4)

indicators.note: Not quite means falling just short of the whole thing, so the word before it arrives one letter light.
A drunk cannot walk a straight line, and letters in that state do not stay in the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: OK is FINE, and this stops short of that word's last letter
eight letters of raw material across the two words, re-sorted

explanation.surface: Checking whether somebody is all right after a bottle of fearsome gin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Demon' describes the gin in the surface and is plain fodder in the wordplay, while the question mark after the first word makes an instruction look like concern.
explanation.definitionFit: Finding Nemo is the Pixar animation about a clownfish father hunting for his lost son, made for and watched by children.

clue.text: Wealthy businessman to surprise, finally, Claude and Hewer (11)

indicators.note: Finally means at the very end, so only the closing letter of the name beside it is taken.

blocks.note: news that rocks you is news that shakes you badly
the last letter of the name, and nothing else from it
a feller brings trees down, which is one way of hewing wood

explanation.surface: A tycoon springing something on two men, Claude and Hewer.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital H makes the last word read as a surname standing beside Claude, which is the whole disguise on a six-letter chunk that is really a job.
explanation.definitionFit: John D. Rockefeller made an oil fortune vast enough that the name became shorthand for a rich businessman, so the definition works by example.

clue.text: In which defence alas is best form of attack? (3,4)

definitions.text: In which defence alas is best form of attack?

blocks.note: the surface offers a maxim about tactics; 'defence' here means the players at the back, the ones furthest from the net they are supposed to be shooting at, and 'alas' is the setter wincing
the saying runs the other way round — attack is the best form of defence — and turned over it describes a defender putting the ball where only the opposition should

explanation.surface: Somebody offering a fresh version of the old sporting maxim about attack and defence.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is printed back to front, and read that way it describes the moment a defender beats his own keeper. 'Alas' is the one word admitting whose misfortune this is.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes the football mishap in which a defending player puts the ball into his own net, so his defending is what produces the other side's score.

clue.text: Loudly criticise a prophet’s cure-all (7)

indicators.note: Something said loudly is said out loud, so what matters is the noise the words make rather than the way they are spelt.

blocks.note: to pan a film is to review it savagely
a prophet is a seer, and in most British speech that final R is not sounded, so what you hear is four more letters

explanation.surface: Shouting down the miracle remedy some prophet is peddling.
explanation.walkthrough: Non-rhotic British speech is what makes this work: the R at the end goes unsounded, so a two-word phrase comes out as the tail of a word about medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: A panacea is a remedy claimed to cure everything, which is what 'cure-all' says — the word is used mostly of solutions that turn out not to work.

clue.text: Facetious chat overcoming resistance; it helps the presentation (4,5)

indicators.note: To come over something is to go over the top of it, so the word beside this closes across the letter named next.

blocks.note: a flip remark is a glib, not-quite-serious one
the clue's own word, used exactly as it stands
R is the physicist's symbol for resistance, as in Ohm's law

explanation.surface: Jokey small talk winning round a reluctant audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overcoming' reads as winning an argument and works as a physical instruction, and the definition is a whole clause rather than a synonym — the object a speaker stands beside.
explanation.definitionFit: A flip chart is the pad of big paper on an easel that a speaker turns over sheet by sheet, so it genuinely helps a presentation along.

clue.text: You can hear part of car stop working (5)

indicators.note: What you can hear is the sound of a word, so the spelling wanted is the other one that makes the same noise.

blocks.note: the pedal that slows a car down, written the other way once only the sound survives

explanation.surface: A noise from somewhere in the car, just before the thing packs up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of car' looks as though it wants a hidden word, since parts of words hide inside phrases all the time. The whole component is meant, and only the noise of its name.
explanation.definitionFit: A machine that breaks has stopped working, so the definition is the intransitive verb — what the car does, not what anyone does to it.

clue.text: Liz refurbished helmet endlessly in ancient town (9)

indicators.note: Something refurbished has been stripped down and put back together looking different, which is what happens to the letters beside it.
Endlessly means without an end, so the final letter of the word it follows is left off.

blocks.note: Liz and Beth are both short for Elizabeth, so either can stand in for the other
six letters with the last one struck off, and the five left over re-sorted

explanation.surface: Liz doing up a helmet, on and on, somewhere very old indeed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refurbished' sits between the two halves and only works on the second. The first is a swap between two pet forms of the same name, which no word in the clue signals at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Bethlehem is the West Bank town thousands of years old, known as the birthplace of King David and of Jesus.

clue.text: Epic tales whichever way you look at it (5)

indicators.text: whichever way you look at it
indicators.note: Reading from either end is the only sense in which a word can be looked at two ways, so the letters have to be symmetrical.

blocks.note: the definition end of the clue: long heroic stories, the Norse ones first of all

explanation.surface: A shrug of a remark: these long dramatic stories are what they are, from any angle.
explanation.walkthrough: Norse literature gives us the word, and it is the plural that makes the symmetry work — the singular would not read the same in both directions.
explanation.definitionFit: A saga is a long heroic narrative, the Icelandic ones above all, and the plural matches 'tales' while 'epic' names their scale.

clue.text: Disdainful son humming (6)

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for son, as written on a family tree
in British slang a thing that is humming smells bad, and niffy says the same — a niff is a nasty smell

explanation.surface: A superior young man who badly needs a wash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Humming' has nothing to do with music here, and both it and its replacement are informal British words for a bad smell, which is what makes the swap fair.
explanation.definitionFit: To be sniffy about something is to look down your nose at it — disdain expressed through the nose, which is also where the smell came in.

clue.text: Time invested in joke by paper that affects current events (3,6)

indicators.note: Money invested in a business goes into it, so the letter named before this ends up inside the word named after.

blocks.note: a jest is a joke
T is the standard abbreviation for time
a ream is five hundred sheets of paper

explanation.surface: Somebody putting time into a gag for a newspaper that shapes the news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paper' looks like a publication and is the physical stuff, sold five hundred sheets at a time, while 'current events' hides a second sense: currents of air, not news.
explanation.definitionFit: The jet stream is the fast ribbon of high-altitude air current that steers weather systems, so it does affect events, and 'current' is the joke.

clue.text: Justice terribly delayed – energy dropping – without enthusiasm (7)

indicators.note: Anything done terribly is done badly, and letters handled badly do not stay in the order they were set down in.
What drops out of something is no longer part of it, so the letter named just before this leaves the material.

blocks.note: J is the standard abbreviation for a judge or justice, printed after the name in law reports
seven letters of raw material with one struck out, and the six left over re-sorted
energy is E to a physicist, and that is the letter taken out of the material

explanation.surface: A court case dragging on while everyone involved runs out of energy.
explanation.walkthrough: Justice delayed is justice denied — the phrase the surface leans on — and the pair of dashes make the middle clause read as a weary aside rather than as an order.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something jadedly is to do it wearily, with the appetite worn out of you, which is doing it without enthusiasm.

clue.text: Told any cobblers in realm of children’s tales? (7)

indicators.note: Cobblers is British slang for rubbish or nonsense, and letters called nonsense are not sitting in any sensible order.

blocks.note: seven letters of raw material across the two words, coming out in a new order

explanation.surface: Accusing somebody of talking rubbish about a storybook world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cobblers' comes from rhyming slang — cobbler's awls — and so means nonsense, which is what lets it order a shuffle while reading as part of the accusation.
explanation.definitionFit: Toyland is the setting of Enid Blyton's Noddy books, the make-believe country those children's stories take place in.

clue.text: 10am, rising, embracing German that’s attractive (6)

indicators.note: A down entry read upwards runs from its foot to its head, and anything that rises travels in exactly that direction.
To embrace someone is to close your arms round them, so whatever is named next finishes up inside.

blocks.note: ten in the morning spelled out gives five letters, then read from the bottom of the column upwards
G is the standard dictionary abbreviation for German

explanation.surface: Someone getting up at ten and hugging a good-looking German.
explanation.walkthrough: The digits have to be spelled out before anything can be done to them, and the clue never says so. 'Attractive' is meant physically rather than as a compliment.
explanation.definitionFit: A magnet is the thing that literally attracts, pulling iron towards it, so 'that's attractive' is the plain physical sense and not the flattering one.

clue.text: Some chic élan demonstrated in Northern location (7)

indicators.note: Some of a thing is a part of it and never the whole, so only a stretch of the words that follow is wanted.

blocks.note: seven consecutive letters run from partway through the first word into the start of the third

explanation.surface: Stylish flair being shown off somewhere well to the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' at the front reads as a quantity of style and is the extraction order, while the italicised French word looks like a definition by example and is only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Iceland is the island republic out in the North Atlantic, further north than anywhere else in Europe, so the definition names it by where it sits.

clue.text: Arouse radiant smouldering – only, naughtily, primarily? (5)

definitions.text: Arouse radiant smouldering – only, naughtily, primarily?

indicators.note: Primarily means in the first place, so only the opening letter of each word it governs is taken.

blocks.note: the letter each of these three words begins with, in the order printed
the opening letter of each of these two words, keeping the run going after the dash

explanation.surface: Someone stirring up a warm glow, and being wicked about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The sentence describes the crime and, taken a letter at a time off the front of each word, spells it. 'Radiant smouldering' is fire being admired rather than reported.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight as a description of the crime: rousing a radiant smouldering, and doing it naughtily, is deliberate fire-raising.

clue.text: Christmas list – piece of cake (4,3)

definitions.note: 'Piece of cake' names a slice while the answer is the whole cake, and the setter is trading on the idiom for something easy, which is where the joke sits.

blocks.note: Yule is the old word for Christmas, still heard in yuletide
a ship's log is the running list of everything that happens aboard

explanation.surface: Working down the Christmas to-do list and finding it no trouble at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece of cake' is an idiom for something easy in the surface and is meant literally in the definition — the chocolate roll iced to look like firewood.
explanation.definitionFit: A yule log is the chocolate-and-cream sponge rolled and iced to resemble a log, eaten at Christmas, so the definition is meant literally.

clue.text: Pursues lost cause – seeks money at proverbial glue factory? (5,1,4,5)

blocks.note: to flog something is to sell it, British slang for shifting goods for cash
the glue factory is where worn-out horses were proverbially sent, so this names what you would find waiting there

explanation.surface: A trader trying to get paid at the place where old horses end up.
explanation.walkthrough: Horses past working age were once sent for rendering into glue, which is why the idiom reaches for a dead one: nothing you do to it will get it moving again.
explanation.definitionFit: To flog a dead horse is to keep pushing at something that cannot go anywhere, which is exactly what pursuing a lost cause amounts to.

clue.text: Begrudge diplomat wanting nothing (4)

indicators.note: Something wanting is missing what it ought to have, so the word beside it turns up short of the letter named next.

blocks.note: an envoy is a diplomat sent out to represent a government
nothing is written as a nought, and that is the letter which goes

explanation.surface: Resenting a diplomat who appears to lack for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanting nothing' reads as a comfortable life and is really an instruction, because wanting here is the older sense of lacking rather than of wishing for.
explanation.definitionFit: To envy someone is to begrudge them what they have — resenting their good fortune, not merely wishing for the same thing yourself.

clue.text: Woman starts to drowse alongside Everyman (4)

indicators.note: A start is a first letter, and the plural of it covers both of the words that follow rather than just the nearer one.

blocks.note: the opening letter of each of these two words
Everyman is the pen name this puzzle's setter signs, so the word means the setter himself

explanation.surface: Nodding off in the seat next to the setter.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters slip themselves into their own clues constantly, and this one's pen name is printed above the grid — so the last word is worth two letters rather than none.
explanation.definitionFit: Dame is an old general word for a woman, and in Britain the formal title given to a woman honoured at the rank of a knight.
